Title: Wizards Emerge as Threat to Jazz's Plan to Keep Walker Kessler

Summary: 
The Washington Wizards are emerging as a serious threat to the Utah Jazz's plans to retain restricted free agent Walker Kessler ahead of the 2026 offseason. Despite Utah's confidence and control over the situation due to restricted free agency—giving them the right to match any offer—the Wizards are widely expected to make a significant offer, according to league sources including Bryson Akins and Tim MacMahon. Kessler, a 7-foot-2 center, has demonstrated elite production, averaging 14.4 points, 10.8 rebounds, and nearly two blocks in five games during the 2025-26 season before a season-ending torn labrum, while also leading the league in offensive rebounds at 4.6 per game. His camp previously sought up to $120 million in total compensation, a figure Utah was unwilling to meet. The Wizards’ acquisition of Trae Young signals a shift from rebuilding to competitiveness, and pairing Young with Kessler would create a potent pick-and-roll engine and strong defensive foundation. With Alex Sarr already leading the league in blocks, moving Sarr to power forward and deploying Kessler at center could solidify Washington’s interior defense. While Utah holds leverage, matching a high-value, front-loaded offer would require significant financial commitment, especially after Kessler’s major shoulder surgery. The decision hinges on whether Utah views Kessler as worth long-term cap sacrifice. As one analysis notes, saying they want to keep him is easy—paying to keep him under pressure from a rival is where the real test begins.

Title: Jazz's Latest Developments Make Walker Kessler Expendable

Summary: 
Jaren Jackson Jr., a 6-foot-10, 242-pound forward-center with a 7-foot-4 wingspan, has been utilized primarily at center (59% of minutes) despite not being a full-time starter at the position. His offensive game is heavily reliant on perimeter shooting—career field goal attempts from beyond the arc range from 24.1% to 48.9%, with 43.7% of his shots taken from at least 10 feet away from the rim. His rebounding and rim protection are inconsistent; at the 2023 FIBA World Cup, he averaged 2.9 rebounds per game and 6.2 rebounds per 36 minutes, underperforming even 6-foot-4 Anthony Edwards. However, Jackson excels defensively as a rim protector, leading the NBA in blocks per game twice—most notably averaging 3.0 blocks in 2022-23, earning Defensive Player of the Year honors. This defensive strength, combined with his size and athleticism, allows him to thrive at center. Meanwhile, Walker Kessler, a 7-foot-2, 245-pound center and 2022-23 All-Rookie selection, averages 9.3 rebounds and 2.4 blocks per game, making him a dominant defensive presence. Yet, with Jackson now capable of protecting the rim at a high level while also threatening from beyond the arc, Kessler’s leverage in negotiations to re-sign with the Utah Jazz has diminished. Jackson’s ability to stretch the floor with his three-point shooting—unlike Kessler, whose outside game remains experimental—makes him a more versatile asset, reducing the Jazz’s urgency to retain Kessler at a premium price.

Title: NBA Trade Rumors 2025-26: While Anthony Davis gets headlines, Mavericks to 'explore' Klay Thompson trade

Summary: 
The NBA trade market for the 2025-26 season is heating up, with front office personnel gathering in Orlando for the G-League Showcase, where trade discussions are intensifying. The Dallas Mavericks, despite having traded Luka Doncic for Anthony Davis (AD), are not merely looking to shed AD’s contract—valued similarly to Giannis Antetokounmpo’s in Milwaukee—but are seeking a 'return of real consequence' in any deal. AD, 32, has played only 12 games this season due to injuries and seeks a contract extension, limiting his trade market. Atlanta, Toronto, and Detroit are among the teams speculated to be interested, though a trade is more likely in the offseason than at the deadline. The Mavericks are also exploring a trade for 35-year-old Klay Thompson, who is averaging 10.8 points, shooting 35.7% from three (but over 40% in his last 10 games), and earning $16.7 million this season with $17.5 million due next year. Interest from Detroit, Memphis, and San Antonio exists, but the Utah Jazz are signaling they will retain Lauri Markkanen and Walker Kessler despite trade interest. Utah holds an 8th-worst record and has a 60.7% chance of keeping its top-eight-protected first-round pick in the draft lottery. Meanwhile, the Clippers, struggling and potentially in rebuild mode, are not open to trading Ivica Zubac, who is averaging 16.2 points, 11.5 rebounds (3rd in the league), and shooting 61.3%—despite defensive focus on him. The Clippers are wary of 'vultures' circling. The Suns are patient on Nick Richards, with trade talks with Toronto on hold. Indiana is seeking a big man, having been rebuffed by Utah on Walker Kessler and engaging Dallas on Daniel Gafford, though the price is steep. The Kings are open to trade talks on Domantas Sabonis, DeMar DeRozan, and Zach LaVine, but are firm on not trading Keegan Murray or rookie Nique Clifford, and are unwilling to attach draft capital to veteran contracts. Keon Ellis is attracting trade interest due to the league’s scarcity of 3-and-D players, but the Kings are not willing to use his contract to sweeten deals. Trade chatter is expected to intensify around Sabonis and Ellis.

Published date: December 19 2025, 19:17

Title: Heat's Nikola Jovic knows he needs to be better. Also, Davion Mitchell doubtful vs. Jazz

Summary: 
Miami Heat forward Nikola Jovic acknowledges his underwhelming performance in the first half of the 2025-2026 NBA season, averaging 8.1 points, 3.7 rebounds, and 2.7 assists per game while shooting 37.1% from the field and just 28.5% from three-point range—ranking fourth-worst among 163 players with at least 130 three-point attempts. Despite signing a four-year, $62.4 million extension in October 2023, Jovic’s production has declined from his career-highs in his prior season. He admitted to struggling with offensive decision-making and spacing, particularly as a center in the Heat’s motion-based offense that lacks traditional screens and handoffs. Jovic emphasized he is self-motivated, stating, 'I drive myself, and I think I'm my biggest motivator.' Heat coach Erik Spoelstra acknowledged Jovic’s struggles but expressed confidence in his ability to grow through adversity, saying, 'He'll be just fine.' Meanwhile, the Heat are expected to be without starting guard Davion Mitchell (sprained left shoulder), listed as doubtful for Saturday’s game against the Utah Jazz, marking his fourth absence in six games. Mitchell, who initially injured his shoulder on January 13, is opting for caution to avoid re-injury. Norman Powell has been upgraded to available after lower back tightness. The Heat will also be without Tyler Herro, Kel’el Ware (hamstring strain), Vlad Goldin, Terry Rozier, and Jahmir Young. The Jazz are similarly depleted, missing Elijah Harkless, Walker Kessler, Kevin Love, Lauri Markkanen, Georges Niang, John Tonje, Oscar Tshiebwe, and Jusuf Nurkic (illness), who is listed as questionable.

Published date: January 24 2026, 19:54

Source: Miami Herald
Classification: Sports
